goal: Replaces Boost.Test with a bespoke, header-only unit-test framework used across the entire C++ test suite.
Aims to unify inconsistent check macros, simplify the depends/guix/vcpkg build, and give the project full control over test tooling.
reviewability: Ready to review, author has been actively addressing feedback with fixes through mid-September.
No open material request is unanswered; a scope question about testing the framework itself is a suggested follow-up, not a blocker.
agreement: Strong concept support from josibake, who wants an in-house framework for future test concurrency work (josibake).

jeanpablojp gave a concept ACK but found several real correctness bugs in the new framework: a segfault on null string comparison, output not flushed on crash, and a silent loss of deterministic random-seed reproduction (jeanpablojp).
Author fixed each of those in subsequent pushes and the discussion shows no standing unresolved objection (rustaceanrob).

result.summary: This PR removes Boost.Test as the unit-test runner for Bitcoin Core and replaces it with a new, header-only, project-specific test framework, plus BOOST_*-compatible macro shims so no test file has to change its assertions. It touches over 160 files, mostly mechanical include swaps produced by a scripted diff, alongside the ~1200-line new framework, associated depends/cmake/vcpkg/guix simplifications, and several fixes for compiler warnings uncovered along the way. It is a continuation of the closed #35587.
result.problem: Boost.Test gives developers four inconsistent ways to write the same assertion with different failure output, adds a real dependency with its own bugs and abandonment risk, and cannot be tailored to Bitcoin Core's needs (per the author and echoed by josibake, who wants a framework flexible enough to support future test-concurrency work).

open_concerns: jeanpablojp's suggestion to add coverage for the new framework's own failure paths (raised 2026-08-30) is an open follow-up idea, not a blocking requirement.

jeanpablojp's question about whether TEST_CASE should delegate to the suite fixture like BOOST_AUTO_TEST_CASE does was answered by the author as an intentional simplification rather than fixed, so it stands as an accepted trade-off.
resolved_concerns: Segfault risk comparing null C-strings under the new decomposition-based check (jeanpablojp) — fixed by adding a null check (rustaceanrob, 2026-09-10).
Test output not flushed before a crash, losing debug context, and duplicated output from forked child processes (jeanpablojp) — fixed with an explicit flush (rustaceanrob, 2026-09-10).

BOOST_TEST_RANDOM seed value was checked only for presence, silently breaking deterministic reproduction of ordering (jeanpablojp) — fixed with proper seed handling and printing (rustaceanrob, 2026-09-10).

std::optional<T> comparisons bypassing the static_assert on missing stringify (jeanpablojp) — acknowledged as the same class of issue as iterator comparisons, to be handled via CHECK_NO_DISPLAY follow-up.
Guix build_linux.sh dropping -Wl,--fatal-warnings for all Linux hosts when removing the riscv64 Boost.Test workaround (jeanpablojp) — addressed by restoring the flag (rustaceanrob, 2026-09-10).

Debate with maflcko over static_assert vs compile failure for missing stringify overloads, and over deleting vs preserving && / || in checks — resolved by implementing a static_assert with CHECK_NO_DISPLAY escape hatch and deleting && / || for correctness (rustaceanrob).

result.card: This PR replaces Boost.Test with a new, project-owned header-only unit-test framework across the entire C++ test suite (163 files, +1696/-264), continuing the closed #35587. It solves real problems with Boost.Test's inconsistent assertion macros and an external dependency the author says has bugs and abandonment risk, a motivation echoed by josibake who wants the flexibility for future test-concurrency work. The strongest evidence of stakes is not the size but the bugs found in review: jeanpablojp identified a segfault on null-string comparisons, output that is never flushed before a crash, and a silently broken deterministic random seed in the new framework itself, all of which the author fixed by 2026-09-10. Reviewability is Ready: the author has been continuously responsive and no material request is unanswered, though the PR is large and still absorbing design feedback (e.g., how to handle types lacking a string representation). No hard dependency blocks it, but it interacts with recent related PRs (#36091, #36018) that were rebased into it.
